I think the best way is to talk with the person in a cooperative way. Let them say what they think and then go through the logical arguments which follow from what they said, with the aim of proving they're wrong by contradiction.

You'll probably run up to a point where they disagree with one of your logical steps, so at this point repeat the process.

If someone says that they need to think about or process what's been said, drop the conversation: this means you've initiated some internal conflict and they will resolve this on their own (or you've just annoyed them to the point where they just want to stop talking to you).

BONUS: The 'debate' style is good for asserting dominance, but pretty useless at convincing people of your opinions.

I learned this primarily from Ancient Greece and my dad:

A well formed argument is like a three-legged stool. It must contain logic (logos), an emotional bond towards your argument (pathos), and a sense of connection to a greater whole in support of your argument (ethos). The stool cannot stand without the support of all three.

When it comes to pace, it's like boiling a frog in water. As morbid as this sounds, a frog will naturally jump out of hot water. However, if you put it in lukewarm water, it will stay even as it slowly intensifies with heat up until the point it is boiled alive. This also applies to the intensity of your argument's progression over time.

When it comes to changing someone's mind, you are in the passenger's seat except you only have control of the steering wheel. You may steer it whichever direction you choose. However, the person you are making the argument to has full control of the brakes and throttle.
